question: A learner wants a 125 cc motorcycle of 10 kW. What is the lowest licence category that covers it?
explanation: Category A1 covers motorcycles of up to 125 cc and 11 kW. AM is for mopeds, and A2 and A cover more powerful machines.

question: Besides engine size, what is the most power a category A1 motorcycle may have?
explanation: A1 motorcycles are limited to 11 kW and a power to weight ratio of 0.1 kW/kg. 35 kW is the A2 limit.

question: You hold an A2 licence. Which motorcycle may you ride on it?
explanation: Category A2 covers motorcycles of up to 35 kW with a power to weight ratio of no more than 0.2 kW/kg. 30 kW and 0.15 kW/kg is within both limits.

question: A dealer offers to restrict a powerful motorcycle so you can ride it on an A2 licence. The machine's original power must not be more than:
explanation: An A2 motorcycle may not be derived from a vehicle of more than double its power. A bike restricted to 35 kW must come from one of no more than 70 kW.

question: You hold a category A2 licence. Which other motorcycles may you ride on it?
explanation: An A2 licence is also valid for A1 motorcycles, and like every motorcycle licence it covers category AM too.

question: A two-wheeler has a 50 cc petrol engine and a top design speed of 45 km/h. For licence purposes it is a:
explanation: Malta's law treats a two-wheeler as a motorcycle only above 50 cc or 45 km/h design speed. Below both, it is a moped in category AM.

question: Which of these does a category AM licence cover?
explanation: Category AM covers mopeds, light quadricycles and electric kick scooters. Motor tricycles and 125 cc motorcycles need an A category.

question: You have a full category A1 licence. Are you allowed to ride a moped?
optionA: No, AM is a separate test
explanation: Licences for categories A1, A2, A and B are all valid for category AM vehicles.

question: A motor tricycle has 20 kW of power. Which licence category does it need?
explanation: Motor tricycles up to 15 kW sit in A1. Above 15 kW they need a full category A licence.

question: On a standard learner's permit, when may you practise riding on public roads?
optionA: Any day of the week, holidays too
explanation: A standard learner's permit allows practice on all days except Sundays and public holidays, under instruction.

question: A friend with a full licence offers to let you ride their motorcycle on your learner's permit, with no instructor. Is this allowed?
optionA: Yes, any licence holder will do
optionB: Yes, if you avoid the main roads
optionD: Yes, as long as it is after dark
explanation: A learner's permit lets you practise under instruction. A friend who is not acting as your instructor does not meet that condition.

question: You ride a category A2 motorcycle and want to move to an unrestricted large bike. What do you need?
explanation: An A2 licence stops at 35 kW. Riding an unrestricted motorcycle needs a category A licence.

question: You hold a full category A licence. Which motorcycles may you also ride?
explanation: A category A licence is valid for categories A1 and A2, and for AM.

question: You hold a full category B car licence. Which of these may you ride on it?
explanation: Licences for categories A1, A2, A and B are also valid for category AM. A motorcycle needs its own A category.

question: Which of these is banned while you ride a motorcycle in Malta?
explanation: Wearing in-ear or over-ear devices in both ears is not allowed while riding a motorcycle or when stopped in traffic, because it shuts out sounds you need.

question: For a rider under 70, how long is a full motorcycle licence valid before it must be renewed?
explanation: Full licences in categories AM, A1, A2, A and B have an administrative validity of ten years, cut to five years once the holder reaches 70.

question: Your motorcycle's insurance ran out yesterday. What should you do before riding it?
optionB: Ride it, there is a grace period
explanation: A motor vehicle must be insured before it is used on the road. An expired policy gives no cover, however short the trip.

question: Your licence shows a condition that you must wear corrective lenses. When does this apply?
explanation: A licence states the conditions on which you may drive or ride. A condition such as corrective lenses applies on every journey.

question: Besides motorcycles, which of these vehicles does Malta's crash helmet law cover?
explanation: No one may drive or be carried on a motorcycle or a quad bike without a crash helmet.

question: With the strap fastened, you can roll a helmet forward off your head. What does this tell you?
explanation: A helmet that can be rolled off with the strap done up is too big and may come off in a crash. Try a smaller size.

question: When is it safe to leave the chin strap of your helmet unfastened?
explanation: An unfastened helmet can come off in the first impact. Fasten the strap every time, however short the trip.

question: Your helmet fell from the seat onto concrete, but no damage shows. What is the safest course?
optionC: Use it only for short trips
explanation: A helmet can be damaged inside with no mark on the outside. A dropped helmet may not protect you properly in a crash.

question: You are offered a cheap second-hand helmet. What is the main risk?
optionD: It will not fit a visor
explanation: You cannot tell whether a used helmet has had an impact that weakened it. Buy new from a source you trust.

question: What should a new motorcycle helmet carry?
optionD: A sticker with your blood group
explanation: Buy a helmet marked as meeting a recognised safety standard. Without approval there is no proof it was impact tested.

question: Your visor is scratched all over. When is this most dangerous?
explanation: Scratches scatter the light of oncoming headlights and street lamps, which can blind you. Replace a scratched visor.

question: You leave work at dusk with a dark visor fitted to your helmet. What should you do?
optionB: Ride with the visor open fast
explanation: A tinted visor makes it hard to see in fading light. Carry a clear visor or ride with a helmet that has a drop-down sun visor.

question: An open-face helmet leaves which part of your head unprotected?
explanation: In a fall the chin often hits the ground first. A full-face helmet covers it; an open-face helmet does not.

question: You want to decorate your helmet. What should you avoid?
explanation: Solvents and some paints can weaken the shell material. Check the maker's guidance before adding anything.

question: Why do riding gloves have extra padding on the palm?
optionA: To grip the fuel tank better
optionC: Hands land on it in a fall
explanation: Riders put their hands out when they fall, so the palm takes the slide. Padding and tough material protect it.

question: Why should riding boots not have long loose laces?
optionC: They let in rain on wet days
optionD: They can catch on the controls
explanation: A lace caught on the footrest or gear lever can stop you putting your foot down. Boots should also cover the ankle.

question: What is the main job of riding trousers and jackets made of leather or abrasion-resistant fabric?
optionA: To resist sliding on the road
optionB: To keep you cooler in summer
optionD: To do the job of a helmet
explanation: Riding gear is made to survive sliding along the road surface, and most have armour at the elbows, shoulders and knees.

question: Malta's summer is very hot. What is the safest choice of riding clothes?
explanation: Mesh or vented riding gear keeps you cooler while still protecting your skin and joints. Bare skin has no protection in a slide.

question: Why might an all-black outfit put you at risk in daytime traffic?
explanation: Dark clothing blends with the road and shadows. Fluorescent colours make you stand out in daylight.

question: What clothing helps other road users see you at night?
explanation: Reflective material returns light from headlights towards the driver. Fluorescent colours do little in the dark.

question: Your visor mists up on a cool, damp morning. What is a safe way to clear it?
optionA: Use an anti-mist insert or vent
optionB: Ride with it fully open at speed
explanation: Anti-mist inserts and helmet vents keep the visor clear. Riding at speed with the visor fully open exposes your eyes to wind and grit.

question: You ride with an open-face helmet. What should you wear to protect your eyes?
explanation: Grit, insects and wind can injure or blind you. Wear approved goggles or a visor with an open-face helmet.

question: How should a helmet sit on your head?
explanation: A helmet tilted back leaves the forehead exposed and can come off. It should sit level, just above your eyebrows.

question: Why do riders wear a back protector or armoured jacket?
optionC: To improve the bike's fuel economy
explanation: Armour spreads the force of an impact. A back protector shields the spine, which a plain jacket does not.

question: Rain is forecast for your ride. What gear will help you ride safely?
explanation: Wet, cold riders lose concentration and feel in their hands. Waterproof gear keeps you alert, and a clear visor lets you see in the gloom.

question: Your passenger only has a cycling helmet. May they ride with you?
optionB: No, a crash helmet is needed
optionC: Yes, on short trips in town
optionD: Yes, if you stay below 50 km/h
explanation: The law requires a crash helmet for anyone carried on a motorcycle. A cycling helmet is not built for motorcycle impacts.

question: Where is the engine cut-out switch usually found?
explanation: The red cut-out switch sits under your right thumb so you can stop the engine without letting go of the bars.

question: Your throttle sticks open while you are riding. Which control stops the engine fastest?
optionC: The fuel tap on the tank
explanation: The cut-out switch is under your right thumb. Use it with the clutch pulled in and brake to a stop.

question: How should you check your motorcycle's engine oil level?
optionC: On level ground, per the handbook
explanation: A bike on a slope gives a false reading. Check on level ground, in the position and at the engine temperature the handbook gives, and top up if the level is low.

question: Your drive chain looks dry and rusty. What should you do?
optionA: Tighten it as far as it goes
explanation: A dry chain wears quickly and can snap or jump off. Clean it, lubricate it and check its tension.

question: What can happen if the drive chain is far too slack?
optionA: It can jump off the sprockets
optionD: The fuel gauge starts reading wrong
explanation: A slack chain can come off and lock the rear wheel. Keep the slack within the figure in the handbook.

question: Where do you find the correct chain slack for your motorcycle?
explanation: Each model has its own figure, measured midway along the lower run of the chain.

question: You plan to check tyre pressures before a ride. When gives the truest reading?
optionB: After an hour in the sun
explanation: Air in a tyre warms and expands as you ride or stand in strong sun, so a warm tyre reads high. Check cold, against the handbook figures.

question: You find a nail in your rear tyre, but it does not seem to have lost air. What should you do?
optionA: Pull it out and ride on
optionB: Ride on until it goes flat
explanation: A puncture can let the tyre deflate suddenly. Have it inspected and repaired or replaced before you ride.

question: The fluid in your front brake reservoir has dropped quickly since last week. What should you suspect?
optionA: A leak or badly worn pads
explanation: The level falls slowly as pads wear, but a quick drop points to a leak. Have the brakes checked before you ride.

question: Before a ride, you check the brake fluid reservoir. What should the level be?
optionC: Right up to the filler cap
explanation: The reservoir has minimum and maximum marks. A low level can mean worn pads or a leak.

question: You twist the throttle and let go, and it stays open. What should you do?
optionD: Ride only on open main roads
explanation: The throttle must snap shut when released. A sticking throttle can take you into a hazard you cannot slow for.

question: Your rear brake light stays dark when you press the pedal, but works with the lever. What should you do?
explanation: Each brake should light the brake light, so drivers behind know you are slowing. A faulty pedal switch should be fixed before you ride.

question: Your steering feels heavy and notchy as you turn the bars. What could be wrong?
explanation: Worn or tight steering head bearings make steering stiff or notchy. They can affect how the bike handles.

question: How should your mirrors be set before you move off?
optionC: Folded in for riding in town
explanation: Set the mirrors while seated so they show as much of the road behind as possible, not your own arms.

question: You park after a ride and see oil dripping under the engine. What should you do?
optionA: Top it up and ignore it
optionD: Ride faster so the oil dries
explanation: Oil on the rear tyre can cause a skid, and a low level damages the engine. Find and fix the leak first.

question: What does the side stand cut-out switch do on many motorcycles?
optionB: Lights a lamp on the stand
optionC: Raises the stand with a motor
optionD: Stops the engine if you ride off
explanation: It cuts the engine if a gear is selected with the stand down, so you cannot ride off with it catching the road.

question: Your motorcycle wobbles at the front at a steady speed on a smooth road. Which check makes sense first?
explanation: Wrong tyre pressures or uneven wear are common causes of instability. Check them before looking further.

question: You have dropped your motorcycle at low speed. What should you check before riding on?
explanation: A fall can bend or snap a lever, the handlebars or a footrest. Check the controls work before riding on.

question: Which warning light should make you stop and check the engine at once?
explanation: An oil pressure warning means the engine may not be lubricated. Stop in a safe place and switch off.

question: Why should you check the horn before a ride?
optionC: It is only needed for the test
optionD: To warn others you are there
explanation: The horn is your way to warn others you are there. Check it works before you need it.

question: Your coolant warning light comes on in heavy summer traffic. What should you do?
optionA: Stop safely and let it cool
optionB: Rev the engine to cool it
optionD: Pour cold water on the engine
explanation: Overheating can damage the engine. Stop somewhere safe, switch off and check the coolant once it has cooled.

question: What do worn brake pads usually cause?
explanation: Worn pads reduce braking and can damage the discs. Check them as part of regular maintenance.

question: As you brake hard on a dry road, where does the motorcycle's weight move?
explanation: Weight moves forward as you brake, pressing the front tyre down. That is why the front brake gives most of the stopping power.

question: How should you apply the front brake in a hard stop?
optionA: Grab it as hard as you can
optionC: Pump it on and off fast
explanation: Squeeze the lever smoothly and build up the pressure as the weight transfers. Grabbing it can lock the front wheel.

question: Why is hard braking while leaned over in a bend risky?
optionC: The tyres have little grip spare
explanation: Leaning uses up much of the tyres' grip. Braking hard as well can make them slide, so brake before the bend while upright.

question: Your front wheel locks under hard braking on a bike without ABS. What should you do?
explanation: A locked front wheel cannot steer and the bike will fall. Release the lever at once, then brake again more gently.

question: What does ABS let you do in a hard stop?
explanation: ABS stops the wheels locking, so you keep steering control. It does not always shorten stopping distances, especially on loose surfaces.

question: You shut the throttle sharply in the middle of a bend. What is likely to happen?
optionB: The bike runs wide or slides
optionC: It leans less and stays upright
explanation: Snapping the throttle shut moves weight forward suddenly and unsettles the tyres. Set your speed before the bend and keep a light, steady throttle through it.

question: A rider stares at a pothole and rides straight into it. What is this called?
explanation: A motorcycle tends to go where the rider looks. Look at the path you want to take, not at the hazard.

question: At normal road speeds, to turn the motorcycle to the right you first press forward on:
explanation: This is counter-steering: a light push forward on the right bar leans the motorcycle to the right and it turns that way.

question: You enter a bend too fast and start to run wide. What is usually the best response?
optionA: Look and lean further into it
explanation: Most bikes can lean further than riders think. Look where you want to go and steer; sudden braking while leaned over can cause a slide.

question: Stopped at traffic lights, why keep your right foot on the pedal?
optionB: To hold the rear brake on
explanation: Your right foot works the rear brake, which holds the motorcycle still. Put your left foot down instead.

question: How do you control speed when riding slowly through a tight car park turn?
optionC: Slip the clutch, light rear brake
optionD: Turn the engine off and coast
explanation: At walking pace, the clutch friction point and a light touch on the rear brake give smooth control. A grab of the front brake on full lock can tip you over.

question: You are moving off uphill from a stop. Which control holds the motorcycle still while you find the friction point?
explanation: Hold the bike on the rear brake, find the clutch friction point, add throttle, then release the brake smoothly.

question: Which gear should you normally select to move off from a stop?
explanation: First gear gives the pull to move off smoothly. Starting in a higher gear can stall the engine or make the motorcycle jerk.

question: You ride down a steep street in Valletta. What helps you keep a steady, low speed?
optionB: A low gear and light braking
explanation: A low gear gives engine braking, with light use of both brakes on top. Coasting in neutral or with the clutch in removes that control.

question: What is the safest way to change down a gear?
optionC: Ease off, clutch in, change down
optionD: Change down halfway through a bend
explanation: Close the throttle, pull in the clutch, select the lower gear and let the clutch out smoothly. Do it before the bend, not in it.

question: Why should you avoid changing gear in the middle of a bend?
optionC: It wastes a lot of fuel
explanation: A jerk from the drive line while leaned over can unsettle the tyres. Choose the right gear before the bend.

question: While making a slow U-turn, what should you avoid?
optionB: Looking where you want to go
optionD: A light touch on the rear brake
explanation: At walking pace with the bars turned, grabbing the front brake can tip the motorcycle over. Control speed with the clutch and rear brake.

question: Your braking distance at 40 km/h on a dry road is about 8 m. About how far is it at 80 km/h?
explanation: Braking distance grows with the square of speed. Twice the speed means about four times the distance: 4 x 8 = 32 m.

question: Your motorcycle weaves at speed with a heavily loaded top box. What is the likely cause?
optionA: Too little fuel in the tank
optionC: Too much weight at the back
explanation: Heavy loads high up and behind the rear wheel lighten the front and can cause weaving. Keep loads low and central.

question: When you approach a hazard, what is meant by covering the brakes?
optionD: Fingers and foot ready on them
explanation: Covering the brakes cuts your reaction time without slowing you before it is needed.

question: Why should you use both brakes together in normal riding?
optionB: It saves wear on the tyres
optionC: It is needed for the ABS
optionD: It turns on the brake light
explanation: Using both brakes spreads the work and keeps the motorcycle steadier. The front still does most of the stopping on a dry road.

question: Your rear wheel starts to slide when you open the throttle on a bend. What is the most likely cause?
optionC: A low level of fuel in the tank
explanation: Harsh acceleration while leaned over asks the rear tyre for more grip than it has. Open the throttle smoothly.

question: When riding slowly in heavy traffic, what helps keep the motorcycle balanced?
optionA: Looking down at the front wheel
explanation: Looking ahead keeps your balance. Riding with your feet down means you cannot use the rear brake or gear lever.

question: You must stop quickly on a dry, straight road. What should you do with the clutch?
optionA: Keep it out to stop sooner
optionC: Use it instead of the brakes
optionD: Pull it in just before stopping
explanation: Brake first and pull in the clutch just before stopping so the engine does not stall. Pulling it in early loses engine braking.

question: What is a good grip on the handlebars?
explanation: A relaxed grip lets the motorcycle steer itself over small bumps. A tight grip passes your tension into the steering.

question: Which control do you normally use to change gear on a manual motorcycle?
explanation: On a manual motorcycle the gear lever is under your left foot and the clutch lever is on the left handlebar.

question: You need to slow down a little for a hazard ahead. What should you do first?
explanation: Check what is behind before you slow down, so you know whether a following vehicle could run into you.

question: On most twist-and-go scooters, the rear brake is worked by:
optionA: A pedal under your right foot
optionB: The lever under your left foot
explanation: On most twist-and-go scooters the rear brake is the left hand lever, because there is no clutch.

question: Why should you not ride with the clutch partly pulled in for long periods?
explanation: Riding on the clutch wears it out and stops the engine helping to control your speed.

question: You approach a sharp left-hand bend you cannot see round. What should you do?
explanation: Choose a speed that lets you stop in the distance you can see is clear. Slow down while upright, before you lean.

question: What is the main risk of riding with the rear brake slightly on all the time?
explanation: Dragging the rear brake heats it, wears it and keeps the brake light on, so drivers behind cannot tell when you are really stopping.

question: You are riding on a narrow road and need to stop quickly. Where should you look?
explanation: Keep your head up and eyes ahead. Looking down makes it harder to keep the motorcycle straight and upright.

question: On a normal two-way road in Malta, where should you usually ride?
optionA: Near the middle of your lane
optionD: In the gutter by the drains
explanation: Riding near the middle of the left lane keeps you clear of drains and debris at the edge and makes you easier to see.

question: You are turning right from a main road into a side street. Where should your motorcycle be as you wait for a gap?
optionD: Out in the middle of the junction
explanation: In left-hand traffic, wait just left of the centre of the road with the wheel straight, so traffic behind can pass on your left.

question: You plan to turn left into a side road. Where should you position?
optionA: Over to the right of the lane
optionC: Towards the left of your lane
explanation: Keep to the left before a left turn, but not so close to the kerb that drains and gravel are a problem.

question: Before turning right off a main road, which last check matters most?
optionB: A look in the left mirror
optionC: A check of the fuel gauge
optionD: A look over your right shoulder
explanation: A rider behind may be overtaking you. The last look over your right shoulder covers the blind spot mirrors miss.

question: You want to overtake a slow van. On which side do you normally pass it?
explanation: Malta drives on the left, so you overtake on the right unless lanes are marked or a vehicle is waiting to turn right.

question: Traffic ahead has stopped in a queue. If you ride past it, which danger should you expect most?
explanation: Drivers in a queue do not expect a motorcycle to pass. Watch for doors, pedestrians crossing between cars and vehicles turning across gaps.

question: Where is it most dangerous to pass a queue of stopped traffic?
optionD: Where you can see well ahead
explanation: Vehicles may turn into or out of the junction through gaps in the queue, straight across your path.

question: When passing slow or stopped traffic, what speed should you keep?
optionA: As fast as the gap allows
optionC: Faster than usual to get past
optionD: Low enough to stop at once
explanation: Keep your speed low enough to stop if a car changes lane or a door opens. The faster you go, the less time you have.

question: Why should you not ride alongside a car for long on a two-lane road?
optionA: You may be in its blind spot
optionB: It wastes a lot of fuel
optionC: It is always against the law
explanation: A driver may not see you beside them and could change lanes into you. Either drop back or pass and move clear.

question: You follow a large lorry. Why should you stay well back?
optionB: So you can see past it
explanation: Hanging back lets you see the road ahead and lets the lorry driver see you in the mirrors.

question: Why should you never wait in the gap on the left of a lorry turning left?
optionA: It will give way to you
optionC: It can crush you as it turns
optionD: The driver can always see you
explanation: Long vehicles swing out before turning left, leaving a gap that closes as they turn. Hold back until the lorry has turned.

question: A car waits to join a roundabout as you ride round it. What tells you first that it is moving out?
explanation: Watch the wheels: they move before a driver who has not seen you pulls out. Be ready to brake.

question: On a roundabout, which vehicles pose a particular danger to a motorcycle?
explanation: Drivers changing lanes or leaving the roundabout may not see a motorcycle. Watch their wheels and position, not only their signals.

question: A bus has stopped at a bus stop ahead on your side. What should you expect?
explanation: People get off and may cross in front of the bus, out of your view. Pass slowly and be ready to stop.

question: After passing a car on your motorcycle, why should you not cut straight back in front of it?
optionB: It is a slow way to pass
optionC: It leaves the driver no gap
explanation: Cutting in close leaves the driver no room if you slow. Move back in only when there is a safe gap ahead of it.

question: Before you overtake, why should you check your mirrors for other motorcycles?
explanation: Motorcycles close up fast. A quick mirror check and a shoulder look stop you pulling out into another rider.

question: Riding in a group, how should each rider decide whether to overtake?
optionD: As soon as one rider goes
explanation: The road may be clear for the rider ahead but not for you. Make your own decision every time.

question: When you stop behind a car in traffic, where should you stop?
optionB: Where you see its rear tyres
explanation: Leaving a gap gives you room to move round it if it breaks down, and space if something comes from behind.

question: A large vehicle overtakes you on an open road. What might you feel?
optionC: A blast of air pushing you
explanation: Large vehicles push air aside, which can move a motorcycle. Keep a firm but relaxed grip and allow for it.

question: You want to change lanes to the right. What is the correct order?
explanation: Check your mirrors, signal, take a look over your right shoulder, then move only if it is safe.

question: Why should a rider check behind before slowing to turn?
optionA: A vehicle may be close behind
optionB: To see if the road is wet
optionC: To check on the passenger's grip
explanation: If a vehicle is following closely, you may need to slow earlier and more gently so it is not caught out.

question: You wait at a busy roundabout entry. Why should you keep your tyres off the dark strip in the middle of the lane?
explanation: Waiting vehicles drip oil and fuel down the middle of the lane, which makes it slippery, worst of all in the wet.

question: Traffic in both lanes is moving slowly. Where should you not ride?
optionB: Behind a car with a gap
optionD: With a gap ahead of you
explanation: Riding fast between moving lanes gives drivers no time to see you before they change lanes.

question: You are approaching a junction where a car waits to pull out. What can you do to be seen?
optionD: Move to where it can see you
explanation: Change your position within the lane so the driver has the best chance of seeing you, and be ready to brake.

question: You see a vehicle ahead waiting to turn right across your path. What should you do?
optionA: Slow and be ready to stop
explanation: The driver may not judge your speed or see you at all. Slow down, cover your brakes and watch the wheels.

question: Why are motorcycles hard for drivers to see at junctions?
optionD: They make no noise at all
explanation: A motorcycle's narrow shape is easily hidden by a window pillar or missed by a driver looking for cars.

question: On a road with parked cars on the left, where should you ride?
explanation: Leave room for a door opening suddenly or a person stepping out from between the cars.

question: A cyclist ahead is riding slowly on a narrow road. How should you pass?
optionC: On the left, by the kerb
optionD: With as much room as a car
explanation: Give a cyclist as much room as you would give a car, and pass only when you can see the road ahead is clear.

question: Why do many riders use dipped headlights in daylight?
explanation: A lit headlight makes a motorcycle stand out against traffic and shadows, so drivers notice it sooner.

question: A driver at a side road looks straight at you, then starts to pull out. What has probably happened?
optionA: They are letting you pass first
optionB: They looked but did not see you
explanation: Drivers often look for cars and miss a motorcycle even when looking its way. Never assume eye contact means you have been seen.

question: A car driver waves you out of a side road into busy traffic. What should you do before you go?
optionA: Go at once, you were invited
optionC: Check the road is clear yourself
optionD: Sound the horn and pull out
explanation: The driver cannot see everything for you, such as a motorcycle overtaking the queue. Make your own checks and go only when it is clear.

question: A driver starts to reverse towards your path without seeing you. What may you do?
optionC: Ride on close behind the car
optionD: Sound your horn to warn them
explanation: The horn is there to warn others of your presence. Be ready to stop as well, as the driver may not hear it.

question: Many motorcycles have indicators that do not cancel themselves. What should you do after a turn?
optionC: Wait for them to time out
explanation: A forgotten indicator may make a driver think you will turn and pull out in front of you.

question: Why are motorcycles hard to see in a car's mirrors?
explanation: A motorcycle can be hidden by a car's pillar or fall in a mirror's blind spot. Stay where drivers can see you.

question: Where should you ride so a driver ahead can see you?
optionC: Where you show in their mirror
explanation: If you can see the driver's face in their mirror, they have a chance to see you.

question: A car ahead signals left at a side road. What should you not assume?
optionB: That its driver has a licence
explanation: A signal may have been left on by mistake. Wait until the car actually starts to turn before you act on it.

question: Why are pedestrians wearing headphones a hazard for riders?
optionA: They may not hear you coming
explanation: People listening to music may step out without hearing traffic. Watch their heads and be ready to slow.

question: A car is reversing out of a driveway ahead. What should you do?
optionD: Sound the horn and speed up
explanation: A reversing driver has a poor view and may not see a motorcycle. Give them time and room.

question: Your helmet muffles traffic noise. What does this mean for you?
optionD: Ride more slowly at night only
explanation: You may not hear other vehicles, so keep scanning and use your mirrors and shoulder checks often.

question: An older pedestrian is crossing slowly as the lights change to green for you. What should you do?
explanation: Pedestrians already crossing must be allowed to finish, however long they take.

question: A horse is being led along the road ahead. What should you avoid as you pass?
explanation: A sudden engine noise can frighten a horse. Pass slowly, wide and quietly.

question: A driver in the car ahead is using a phone and drifting in the lane. What should you do?
explanation: A distracted driver is unpredictable. Keep well back until you can pass safely or they move away.

question: Why are motorcycles at greater risk than cars in a collision?
explanation: A rider takes the impact directly, so riding defensively and being seen matter even more.

question: What is meant by riding defensively?
explanation: A defensive rider looks well ahead, plans for what others might do and leaves room to react.

question: An ice-cream van is parked by the road with its music playing. What should you expect?
explanation: Children may run to or from the van without looking. Slow down and be ready to stop.

question: A car ahead slows suddenly and its driver looks at the house numbers. What should you expect?
optionB: It may stop or turn suddenly
optionD: It will move to the right lane
explanation: Drivers looking for an address often stop or turn suddenly. Keep back until you can see what they will do.

question: You are in a slow queue on your motorcycle when an ambulance with a siren comes up behind. What should you do?
optionA: Ride ahead of it at speed
optionC: Move aside where it is safe
explanation: Make room for the ambulance in a safe way: a narrow motorcycle can easily block the gap it needs. Do not break the law or put others in danger to do it.

question: A goat has strayed onto a rural road in Gozo ahead of you. What should you do?
optionB: Rev the engine to scare it
explanation: An animal can move into your path without warning, and hitting even a small one can bring a motorcycle down. Slow down and give it room.

question: Why is it dangerous to ride fast through slow-moving town traffic?
explanation: Drivers judge gaps by the traffic they expect. A fast motorcycle arrives before they think it will.

question: A delivery van has stopped half on the pavement ahead. What hazard should you expect?
explanation: Delivery drivers often get out quickly, sometimes on the road side. Pass with room and be ready to stop.

question: Which part of the road is most slippery for a motorcycle after rain?
explanation: Drain and manhole covers give very little grip when wet. Avoid riding over them while braking or leaning.

question: It is raining as you reach a zebra crossing. Where is grip lowest?
explanation: Painted markings give less grip than tarmac, especially when wet. Stay upright and avoid braking on them.

question: A light shower falls on a hot August afternoon after weeks without rain. How should you ride?
optionA: As usual, it is only light
optionB: Faster, to get home before it
explanation: A first shower mixes with the oil, rubber and dust baked onto the road into a greasy film. Grip is often at its worst early on.

question: Where are diesel spills most often found?
optionB: In the middle of large car parks
explanation: Diesel slops from overfilled tanks on bends and roundabouts near fuel stations. Look for a rainbow sheen and avoid it.

question: Sand has blown onto a coast road. How should you ride over it?
explanation: Loose sand and gravel reduce grip. Ride smoothly and upright, and make any braking or steering before you reach it.

question: You ride on a smooth limestone or paved street in an old town after rain. What should you expect?
explanation: Polished stone and paving can become very slippery when wet. Slow down and avoid sudden actions.

question: Heavy spray from a lorry ahead keeps covering your visor in the rain. What should you do?
optionC: Drop back out of the spray
optionD: Wipe it with your gloved hand
explanation: Dropping back clears your view and gives you more room to stop on the wet road.

question: Strong crosswinds are blowing on an exposed coast road. Where are you most likely to be blown off course?
explanation: Wind gusts through gaps between buildings and at open stretches. Expect sudden pushes and keep speed down.

question: After riding through deep water, your brakes feel weak. Why?
optionA: The discs and pads are wet
explanation: Water on the brakes reduces their grip. Brake gently a few times when it is safe to dry them out.

question: There is loose gravel on a bend ahead. What is the safest approach?
optionD: Speed up to skim over it
explanation: Loose surfaces give little grip in a bend. Slow down while upright and keep your lean and braking gentle.

question: Why can freshly laid tarmac be dangerous on a hot summer day?
optionC: It can be soft and greasy
optionD: It cools your tyres too much
explanation: In strong heat the surface can soften and bring up a slippery binder. Ride smoothly and avoid sharp turns.

question: Salt spray from rough seas has smeared your visor on a coast road. What should you do?
explanation: Salt spray dries into a film that scatters light. Stop somewhere safe and clean the visor so you can see properly.

question: At night, why can drivers misjudge an approaching motorcycle?
optionA: One headlight is hard to judge
explanation: A single headlight gives few clues about distance and speed, so a driver may pull out thinking you are further away.

question: Entering a road tunnel on a sunny day, what should you do with your visor?
explanation: A dark visor makes the tunnel very dim. Use a clear visor or lift the sun visor before you enter, and switch on dipped lights.

question: The sun is low in the sky behind you. Why may drivers coming towards you not see you?
optionC: They are dazzled by the sun
explanation: With the sun in their eyes, oncoming drivers may not see a motorcycle at all. Be ready for them to turn across you.

question: Standing water lies across a bend in heavy rain. What is the main danger?
explanation: At speed the tyres can ride up on the water and lose grip, which is called aquaplaning. Slow down before you reach it.

question: Why are tyres and brakes less effective when cold?
explanation: Tyres need a few kilometres to warm up. Ride gently at first, especially on a cool morning.

question: Riding at night, why should you ride more slowly than in daylight?
optionB: You can see less far ahead
optionD: Roads are always wet at night
explanation: You must be able to stop within the distance your headlight shows is clear.

question: You ride along a road with ruts made by heavy lorries. What is the risk?
explanation: Ruts can steer your wheels. Ride smoothly, avoid crossing them at a shallow angle and keep a relaxed grip.

question: There is a pothole ahead. What is the safest action?
explanation: Look well ahead so you can change position smoothly. A late swerve can put you in the path of other traffic.

question: You must ride on a wet road. Which riding style gives most grip?
explanation: In the wet, every action should be gentle and gradual. Sudden inputs can break the tyres' grip.

question: Why should you take extra care on bends on country roads at night?
explanation: A headlight points straight ahead, so on a bend it shows less of where you are going. Slow down.

question: Two friends both ask for a lift on your motorcycle at the same time. What does the law allow?
explanation: The law allows no more than one person besides the rider on a motorcycle.

question: Where must a passenger's seat be on a motorcycle?
optionC: On top of the fuel tank
explanation: A passenger must sit astride on a proper seat securely fixed to the motorcycle behind the rider's seat.

question: How should you park a motorcycle at the side of a street in Malta?
optionC: At an angle to the kerb
explanation: Motorcycles must not be parked parallel to the kerb or wall, but at an angle of at least 45 degrees to it.

question: Your passenger leans the opposite way to you in bends. What happens?
optionD: The bike is harder to steer
explanation: A passenger who leans against the turn fights your steering. Ask them to lean with you and the motorcycle.

question: You stop at traffic lights with a passenger. Who should hold the motorcycle up?
explanation: The rider supports the motorcycle when stopped. A passenger who puts a foot down can unbalance it, so they keep their feet on the footrests.

question: Your handbook gives two sets of tyre pressures. When do you use the higher ones?
optionC: Only on short trips in town
explanation: Extra weight needs higher pressures, and often a suspension change too. The handbook gives both.

question: With a passenger on board, how should you plan your stops?
explanation: The extra weight means the motorcycle takes longer to stop. Leave more room and brake earlier and more smoothly.

question: Where should luggage be carried on a motorcycle?
explanation: Low, central and balanced loads affect handling least. Bags on the handlebars can affect the steering.

question: You fit panniers to your motorcycle. What should you check?
optionC: They are full to the top
explanation: Uneven panniers pull the motorcycle to one side and upset its balance.

question: You park on a very hot day on soft tarmac. What could happen to the side stand?
optionB: It can sink and the bike fall
optionC: It will get hotter than the engine
explanation: Heat softens tarmac, so a stand can sink. Use a flat plate under it or park on firm ground.

question: What should you do every time you leave your motorcycle parked?
optionA: Leave the key in for others
optionC: Lock it and take the key
explanation: Locking the steering and taking the key makes theft harder. Use a disc lock or chain too if you can.

question: Before you carry a passenger for the first time, what should you tell them?
optionD: How to sit and move with you
explanation: A passenger who knows to hold on, lean with you and keep their feet on the footrests helps you ride safely.

question: A passenger's feet cannot reach the footrests. Should you carry them?
optionB: Yes, if they hold on tight
explanation: A passenger sits astride on a proper seat and needs to rest their feet on the footrests. Without them they cannot stay stable or move with you in bends.

question: You plan a long trip with a full top box. What should you check in the top box handbook?
explanation: Top boxes and racks have a weight limit. Heavy loads high and behind the rear wheel make the front feel light.

question: Why is alcohol especially dangerous for a rider?
explanation: Alcohol slows reactions and affects balance and judgement. A rider depends on balance even more than a driver.

question: You had a few drinks last night. What is true the next morning?
explanation: Your body clears alcohol slowly. You may still be over the limit and impaired the next morning.

question: How can illegal drugs affect a rider?
explanation: Drugs can slow reactions, distort how you judge speed and distance, and make you take risks. Their effects can last for days.

question: Why can a long motorcycle ride tire you more than the same trip by car?
explanation: Wind, noise and vibration wear you down. Plan regular stops and rest as soon as you feel drowsy.

question: Why is dehydration a risk when riding in Malta's summer heat?
optionD: It has no effect at all
explanation: Heat and riding gear make you sweat. Drink water before and during rides to stay alert.

question: A driver cuts you up and you feel your temper rise. What is the safest response?
optionA: Chase them to make a point
optionB: Let it go and drop back
optionD: Sound the horn all the way
explanation: Anger makes you take risks and miss hazards. Drop back, calm down and ride on at your own pace.

question: Your phone sits in a handlebar mount for navigation. When may you touch it to change the route?
explanation: Holding or using a hand-held device while riding, or while stopped in traffic, is against the law. Park safely first.

question: You stop to help at a crash. Where should you leave your motorcycle?
optionA: Across the lane as a barrier
optionC: In the middle of the road
explanation: Park well clear so your motorcycle does not cause a second crash or block emergency vehicles.

question: A rider who fell has a suspected broken leg. What should you do?
explanation: Moving a broken limb can make the injury worse. Keep the casualty still and comfortable until help arrives.

question: An injured motorcyclist is lying in the road, conscious and breathing. Should you take off their helmet?
explanation: Removing a helmet can make a neck injury worse. Leave it on unless the casualty cannot breathe properly.

question: While parking, you knock over another motorcycle and damage it. Its owner is nowhere to be found. What should you do?
explanation: If you cause damage and cannot find the owner, report it to the police so it can be dealt with properly.

question: After a crash, petrol is leaking from a motorcycle. What should you not allow?
explanation: Leaking fuel can catch fire. Switch off engines and keep anyone smoking away.

question: New riders are involved in more crashes. What is the main reason?
explanation: New riders have not yet learned to spot hazards early. Ride within your ability and keep learning.

question: What is reaction time?
optionC: Time the brakes take to cool
explanation: Your reaction time adds to your stopping distance. Tiredness, alcohol and distraction all make it longer.

question: A friend riding with you keeps urging you to go faster. What should you do?
optionC: Ride at your own safe pace
optionD: Ride close on their back wheel
explanation: Ride at a speed that suits you, the road and the conditions. Let others ride on.

question: How does cold weather affect a rider without proper gear?
explanation: Cold hands lose feeling and strength on the controls, and the cold tires you. Wear warm, windproof gear.

question: You are taking medicine on prescription. Who can tell you if it affects riding?
explanation: Your doctor or pharmacist can say whether a medicine affects your ability to ride safely.

question: A crash casualty is awake but pale, cold and shaking. What helps while you wait?
explanation: These are signs of shock. Keep the casualty warm and reassured, and give nothing to eat or drink.

question: Why is it dangerous to ride with music playing in your helmet?
explanation: Music hides sirens, horns and engine sounds that warn you of hazards.

question: You feel unwell with a heavy cold. What is the safest choice?
explanation: Illness slows your reactions and concentration. Use other transport until you feel well.
